title: Agency and principal disbursements, and VAT
subtitle: Why two payments made on the client's behalf can attract completely different VAT treatment
objectives: Distinguish an agency disbursement from a principal disbursement by reference to who actually contracts with the supplier
Explain why VAT treatment diverges between the two categories: no VAT added by the firm on an agency disbursement, but input VAT reclaimed and output VAT charged on rebilling a principal disbursement
Apply the distinction to a fact pattern to identify the correct bookkeeping and billing treatment for a disbursement, including the figures involved

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out HMRC's multi-factor test for treating a payment as a disbursement for VAT purposes
Governs use of the client account, including payment of disbursements on a client's behalf

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can define 'disbursement' in the abstract. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the definition — this lesson is about picking the right one under exam pressure, with numbers attached.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the underlying VAT rule here before. The test pool below leans on fact patterns with real figures — expect to work out amounts, not just recite the rule.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 2 and Part 3 and hold the two definitions side by side before moving on — the rest of the lesson assumes you can state both without hesitating.

overview.hook: A conveyancing firm pays a Land Registry fee of £135 and a surveyor's valuation fee of £600 on the same file, on the same day, both described in the file note as 'paid on the client's behalf'. One goes on the bill with no VAT added. The other goes on the bill with £120 of VAT added on top. Nothing about the amount, or the fact that the firm wrote the cheque, explains the difference — and getting it backwards means either short-changing HMRC or over-charging the client.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. HMRC's disbursement test (VAT Notice 700, para 25.1) is a multi-factor, evidential test rather than a bright-line rule, and genuinely borderline categories exist — search fees bought through a search agent and medical records fees are two the profession and HMRC have not always agreed on. Where this lesson flags a category as borderline, treat that as an honest description of the state of the guidance, not an examiner's trick.

parts.heading: Two disbursements, same invoice, different treatment
parts.voice: contrastive — sets up two payments that look identical but aren't
body: A firm acting on a conveyancing matter pays a Land Registry fee of £135 and pays an independent surveyor £600 for a valuation report the client asked for. Both payments leave the firm's bank account for the client's benefit. Both end up as separate lines on the final bill. Yet the Land Registry fee is added to the bill with no VAT charged by the firm at all, while the surveyor's fee is added with 20% VAT on top — an extra £120 the client did not expect from reading the surveyor's own invoice.

The difference has nothing to do with size, purpose, or who physically wrote the cheque. It turns entirely on one question: who did the supplier actually contract with — the client, or the firm? Answer that correctly and the bookkeeping and VAT treatment follow automatically. Answer it wrongly and a firm either under-declares VAT it owes HMRC, or overcharges a client for VAT that was never actually due.

This lesson works both categories through side by side, because the recurring SQE1 trap is the same one every time: a fact pattern describes a payment made 'on the client's behalf' and invites you to assume that phrase settles the question. It doesn't. 'On the client's behalf' describes who benefits — not who contracted with the supplier, which is the only fact that actually matters here.

components.definition: A payment a firm makes on a client's matter to a third party — court fees, search fees, expert fees, counsel's fees and the like. The word covers both agency and principal disbursements; it does not by itself tell you which category applies or how VAT is charged on rebilling it.

interaction.prompt: A firm pays a fee to a third party 'on the client's behalf'. Does that phrase, by itself, tell you whether the payment is an agency or a principal disbursement?
options: No — it only tells you who benefits; the category depends on who the supplier contracted with
Yes — anything paid on the client's behalf is automatically an agency disbursement
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. 'On the client's behalf' is true of almost every disbursement, agency or principal — it settles nothing about VAT.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — that phrase is true of both categories. The category turns on the contractual relationship between the supplier and the client or firm, which you'll work through next.

parts.heading: The agency disbursement: the supplier contracts with the client
parts.voice: structural — builds the definition as a checklist
body: An agency disbursement arises where the supplier's contract is genuinely with the client, and the firm is merely the conduit through which the client's own money passes — acting, in VAT terms, as the client's agent rather than as a party to the supply itself. A Land Registry fee is the textbook example: the client is the applicant, the fee is the client's own statutory liability, and the firm simply pays it and is reimbursed.

Because the firm is not itself receiving a supply for its own business, it adds nothing to the figure and charges no VAT of its own on it. The exact amount the supplier charged is passed straight through to the client's bill, itemised separately, with no mark-up and no VAT layered on top — even where the underlying fee itself includes VAT charged by the supplier to the client.

HMRC's guidance (VAT Notice 700, para 25.1) sets out the factors that point towards a payment qualifying as a disbursement for VAT purposes: the client authorised the payment in advance; the supplier's own invoice is addressed to, or otherwise identifies, the client as the customer; the exact amount is passed on unchanged; and the item is shown separately on the firm's bill rather than folded into the fee for legal services.

components.label: Hallmarks of an agency disbursement
points: The client authorised the specific payment in advance
The supplier's invoice is addressed to, or otherwise identifies, the client — not the firm — as the customer
The exact amount paid to the supplier is passed on unchanged, with no mark-up
The item is shown separately on the bill, distinct from the firm's own fees
The firm has not used the item itself in providing its own service — it has simply paid the client's own liability

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly marks this out as an agency disbursement.
interaction.scenarioText: A firm applies to the Land Registry for official copies of a title, at the client's request. The Land Registry issues its fee invoice addressed to the applicant client, for the exact statutory fee of £3. The firm pays it from the client account and lists it separately on the bill at £3, with no VAT added.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the key hallmark — the supplier's own invoice names the client, not the firm, as its customer. Everything else (no mark-up, no VAT) follows from that.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at who the Land Registry's invoice is actually addressed to — that is what fixes the contractual relationship, and everything about the VAT treatment follows from it.

parts.heading: The principal disbursement: the supplier contracts with the firm
parts.voice: technical — works through the mechanics with real figures
body: A principal disbursement arises where the supplier actually contracts with the firm, not the client — the firm is the customer, receives the supply for its own business purposes, and then recharges the cost to the client as part of providing its overall legal service. A document-review contractor engaged by the firm, or a courier the firm books in its own name, are typical examples.

Because the firm is the true customer, it is entitled to reclaim any input VAT the supplier charged it, and it must then charge output VAT when it rebills the cost to the client — the rebilled amount becomes part of the firm's own supply of legal services, VAT-rated at the standard rate regardless of what VAT (if any) the original supplier charged.

Work the numbers through: the firm engages a document management contractor who invoices the firm £500 plus £100 VAT, total £600. The firm pays the full £600, but reclaims the £100 input VAT from HMRC on its own VAT return — the net cost to the firm is £500. When the firm bills the client, it rebills £500 plus its own output VAT of £100 (20%), so the client pays £600 — the same cash figure, but as a supply from the firm, not a pass-through of the contractor's invoice.

components.text: A payment only qualifies as a disbursement for VAT purposes where the firm acted as the client's agent in making it. Where the firm is itself the recipient of the supply — because it, not the client, is the customer named on the supplier's invoice, and it uses the item for its own business in providing legal services — the payment is not a disbursement: it is a cost component of the firm's own supply, and VAT is charged on the full rebilled amount.
elements: Firm is the named customer on the supplier's invoice
Firm uses the item for its own business purpose
Firm reclaims input VAT charged by the supplier
Firm charges output VAT on the full amount rebilled to the client

interaction.prompt: A firm books a courier in its own name to deliver a completed set of documents, and pays the courier's invoice of £40 plus £8 VAT. How should the firm treat this when billing the client?
options: Pass on exactly £48 with no further VAT, as an agency disbursement
Reclaim the £8 input VAT, then rebill the client £40 plus its own 20% output VAT
Reclaim the £8 input VAT and rebill the client only £40, absorbing the VAT saving
interaction.explanation: The courier's contract is with the firm, not the client, so this is a principal disbursement: the firm reclaims the input VAT the courier charged it, and charges its own output VAT when it rebills the net cost as part of its bill.

parts.heading: The same transaction, worked two ways
parts.voice: worked-example — compares the two treatments side by side
body: Take a medical records fee on a personal injury file: a GP practice charges £50 for copying a client's medical records. If the client instructed the GP practice directly and the firm merely arranges payment on the client's authority, with the GP's invoice addressed to the client, this is an agency disbursement — the firm pays £50 from the client account and bills the client £50, no VAT added (GP records fees are, in any event, usually VAT-exempt at source, which only reinforces the point).

Change one fact: the firm itself instructs a records-retrieval agency, in the firm's own name, to obtain the records as part of preparing the case, and that agency charges the firm £50 plus £10 VAT. Now the firm is the customer. It reclaims the £10 input VAT, and rebills the client £50 plus its own £10 output VAT — £60 on the bill, not £50, even though the client's underlying need (a copy of their medical records) was identical in both versions.

This is why the contractual question has to be asked transaction by transaction, not category by category. 'Medical records fee' is not itself an answer — the same label can sit on either side of the line depending on who the supplier's invoice actually names.

components.title: Agency or principal? A decision path
components.description: A flowchart used to classify a disbursement for VAT purposes.

nodes.label: Who does the supplier's invoice name as the customer?
The client → check: did the client authorise it, and is the exact amount passed on unchanged?
The firm → the firm is the true recipient of the supply
Agency disbursement — pass on the exact amount, no VAT added by the firm
Principal disbursement — reclaim input VAT, then rebill with the firm's own output VAT

components.textAlternative: First ask who the supplier's invoice names as the customer. If the client is named, and the client authorised the payment with the exact amount passed on unchanged, treat it as an agency disbursement: pass on the exact figure with no VAT added by the firm. If the firm is named as the customer, it is a principal disbursement: the firm reclaims any input VAT charged by the supplier, then rebills the net cost plus its own output VAT as part of its bill for legal services.

interaction.prompt: Two medical records requests on the same type of file. In which is this a principal disbursement?
interaction.scenarioA: The client instructs the hospital directly to release records to the firm; the hospital's invoice for £45 is addressed to the client, and the firm pays it and bills the client £45 with no VAT added.
interaction.scenarioB: The firm instructs a records-retrieval company in its own name to obtain the same records for use in preparing the case; the company invoices the firm £45 plus £9 VAT.
interaction.explanation: In B the supplier's invoice names the firm, not the client, as customer — the firm is using the records for its own purposes in preparing the case. That makes it a principal disbursement: input VAT reclaimed, output VAT charged on rebilling. In A the hospital's invoice names the client, which points to an agency disbursement.

parts.heading: VAT Notice 700: a test of factors, not a bright line
parts.voice: honest — names the genuinely contested edge cases rather than smoothing them over
body: It's worth being precise about what HMRC's test actually is, because SQE1 fact patterns sometimes sit close to the boundary on purpose. VAT Notice 700, para 25.1 does not lay down a single decisive fact — it lists indicators (client authorisation, invoice addressee, exact pass-through amount, separate itemisation, no use by the firm for its own purposes) and the overall picture has to point towards agency for the payment to be treated as a disbursement. No single indicator is automatically conclusive on its own.

This is why two categories remain genuinely argued over in practice rather than settled: search fees bought through a search agent (where the agent's own charge is sometimes bundled with the underlying local authority fee), and medical records fees requested through an intermediary service rather than directly from the records holder. Firms take different, defensible positions on both. Treat any exam fact pattern that sits close to this boundary as testing whether you can apply the factors, not as expecting you to know a rule that does not exist.

SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 4 sits alongside this: it governs how a firm may use the client account to pay a disbursement in the first place — including a rule that a firm generally should not pay a disbursement from the client account before it is actually due, or before the client's money to cover it is in the account — but r 4 itself says nothing about VAT. The two questions (may the firm pay it from client account now, and how is VAT charged on it) are answered by two entirely different sources and should not be conflated.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often reason: 'the firm paid it, so the firm must have contracted for it, so VAT applies.'
components.whyItsWrong: Who physically makes the payment is irrelevant — a firm routinely pays agency disbursements too, out of the client account, precisely because it is convenient for the client. The only question that decides VAT treatment is who the supplier's own invoice treats as its customer.

interaction.prompt: Under VAT Notice 700, para 25.1, which single fact is, on its own, automatically conclusive that a payment is an agency disbursement?
options: The fact that the client ultimately benefits from the payment
No single fact is automatically conclusive — HMRC weighs a set of indicators together
The fact that the firm paid the supplier from the client account
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the test is evidential. Authorisation, invoice addressee, exact pass-through and separate itemisation are all weighed together; none alone settles it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Neither of those facts is decisive on its own — both are true of many principal disbursements too. HMRC's test weighs several indicators together rather than turning on one fact.

testPool.prompt: A firm pays a court issue fee of £455 that the client owes directly to HM Courts & Tribunals Service, with the court's own fee notice addressed to the client as the party bringing the claim. How should this appear on the firm's bill?
options: Added at £455, with no VAT charged by the firm
Added at £455 plus 20% VAT charged by the firm
Added at £455 plus the firm's standard mark-up for arranging payment
Not shown on the bill at all, since it is a statutory fee
testPool.explanation: A court fee owed directly by the client, with the fee notice addressed to the client, is a textbook agency disbursement: the exact amount is passed on with no VAT added by the firm.

testPool.prompt: Which fact is the single most important indicator in deciding whether a payment is an agency disbursement rather than a principal disbursement?
options: The size of the payment
Whether the client ultimately pays for it
Who the supplier's invoice names as its customer
Whether the payment is made from the client account or the business account
testPool.explanation: The supplier's own contractual relationship — who they invoice as their customer — is the decisive factor. Size, ultimate payer and which account the payment is made from are all consistent with either category.

testPool.prompt: A firm's costs draftsman is engaged and invoiced in the firm's own name for £300 plus £60 VAT to prepare a bill of costs, which the firm then recharges to the client as part of its overall bill. Which of the following best describes the correct VAT treatment?
options: Agency disbursement: pass on £360 unchanged, no further VAT
Principal disbursement: reclaim the £60 input VAT and rebill £300 plus the firm's own output VAT
No disbursement at all — costs draftsman fees can never be recharged to a client
Principal disbursement, but VAT is only charged if the client is itself VAT-registered
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting error is to treat the draftsman's invoice as something simply passed through because it is calculated as a fixed professional fee. But the draftsman contracted with the firm, not the client — so the firm reclaims the input VAT and charges its own output VAT on rebilling, regardless of the client's own VAT status.
testPool.explanation: Because the invoice names the firm as customer, this is a principal disbursement, handled exactly as any other cost of providing the firm's own service.

testPool.prompt: A trainee notes on file: 'Paid search fee £120 on client's behalf, added to bill at £120, no VAT.' The supplier's invoice was in fact addressed to the firm, not the client, and the firm used the results in preparing its own advice. What is the effect of the trainee's treatment?
options: It is correct — anything described as paid 'on the client's behalf' is automatically VAT-free
It understates the bill — the firm should have reclaimed input VAT and charged output VAT on rebilling
It overstates the bill — no VAT should have been charged and the fee should have been reduced
It is correct, provided the client is told separately that VAT may apply later
testPool.trapExplanation: The phrase 'on the client's behalf' is being treated as decisive, but it isn't — the invoice addressee shows the firm was the true customer. Where the firm is the customer, output VAT should have been charged on rebilling; omitting it means the firm has under-billed the client and under-declared output VAT to HMRC.
testPool.explanation: Because the supplier invoiced the firm and the firm used the search for its own advice, this was a principal disbursement mislabelled as an agency one — the correct bill should have included the firm's own output VAT.

testPool.prompt: A firm engages a translation agency in its own name to translate a set of documents. The agency invoices the firm £200 plus £40 VAT. How much output VAT should the firm charge when it rebills this cost to the client?
options: £40, calculated on the net £200
No output VAT — the input VAT already covers it
£48, calculated on the gross £240
The firm should simply pass on £240 with no VAT of its own added
testPool.explanation: This is a principal disbursement. The firm reclaims the £40 input VAT the agency charged it, then charges its own 20% output VAT on the net £200 when rebilling — £40 output VAT, so the client is billed £240 as part of the firm's own supply.

testPool.prompt: A client asks the firm to arrange for an independent expert to prepare a report and pay the expert directly. The expert's invoice, at the client's request, is addressed to the client personally, and states the exact fee as £800 (the expert is not VAT-registered). The firm pays £800 from the client account. What figure should appear on the client's bill for this item, and how?
options: £800, itemised separately, with no VAT added by the firm
£800 plus the firm's 20% output VAT, itemised as part of the firm's fees
£960 (£800 plus VAT at 20%), itemised separately
£800, folded into the firm's own professional fee rather than itemised separately
testPool.explanation: The invoice is addressed to the client, the client authorised the specific arrangement, and the exact amount is passed on unchanged — an agency disbursement, itemised separately with no VAT added by the firm (and there is no VAT to add in any event, since the expert is not VAT-registered).

testPool.prompt: A firm books a process server in its own name to serve proceedings, and is invoiced £75 plus £15 VAT. The firm's bookkeeper simply enters £90 on the bill with no further VAT, reasoning that VAT has 'already been paid'. What is wrong with this treatment?
options: Nothing — charging VAT twice would be unlawful
The firm should have reclaimed the £15 input VAT and charged its own output VAT of £15 on the net £75, billing £90 as part of its own supply rather than a straight pass-through
The firm should have billed only £75, since VAT is never chargeable on disbursements
The firm should have billed £105, adding a second 20% VAT charge on top of the £90
testPool.explanation: Because the process server's invoice names the firm, this is a principal disbursement. The end figure of £90 happens to be numerically the same either way here, but the correct route is to reclaim the £15 input VAT and charge £15 output VAT on rebilling — not to treat the supplier's invoice as simply passed through.

testPool.prompt: Under VAT Notice 700, para 25.1, which of the following is NOT one of the indicators HMRC weighs in deciding whether a payment is an agency disbursement?
options: Whether the client authorised the specific payment in advance
Whether the supplier's invoice identifies the client, rather than the firm, as its customer
Whether the amount is shown separately on the bill rather than folded into the firm's fees
Whether the firm ultimately made a profit on its overall retainer with the client
testPool.explanation: The firm's overall profitability on the retainer has nothing to do with the disbursement test, which looks only at the specific transaction — authorisation, invoice addressee, exact pass-through, separate itemisation, and whether the firm used the item for its own purposes.

testPool.prompt: SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 4 and VAT Notice 700, para 25.1 both bear on how a firm handles a disbursement. Which best describes the relationship between them?
options: They are the same rule expressed in two different documents

R 4 governs whether and when the firm may pay the disbursement from the client account; VAT Notice 700 separately governs how VAT is charged when the cost is rebilled — the two questions are independent
VAT Notice 700 overrides r 4 wherever the two appear to conflict
R 4 only applies to principal disbursements, and VAT Notice 700 only applies to agency disbursements
testPool.explanation: R 4 is about the mechanics of paying from the client account (and the SRA's restriction on paying a disbursement before it is actually due); VAT Notice 700 is about HMRC's separate question of VAT treatment on rebilling. Neither displaces the other, and both can apply to the same payment.

testPool.prompt: A firm's finance manager says: 'If HMRC's factors don't clearly point one way, we can just choose whichever VAT treatment is more convenient for the client.' Is this consistent with VAT Notice 700?
options: Yes — the client's preference is the deciding factor in a genuinely borderline case
No — the firm must apply the factors honestly to the actual facts of the transaction; a borderline case still has a correct answer, even if it takes more care to reach
Yes — firms are given a free choice between the two treatments for administrative convenience
No — in any borderline case the payment must always be treated as a principal disbursement by default
testPool.explanation: There is no default rule for borderline cases and no discretion to pick whichever suits the client. The firm has to weigh the actual facts (authorisation, invoice addressee, use of the item) honestly — borderline just means the analysis takes more care, not that the outcome is optional.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the correct description of how input VAT works for a principal disbursement?
options: The firm never recovers VAT charged by the supplier on a principal disbursement
The firm reclaims the VAT the supplier charged it as input VAT on its own VAT return, then charges output VAT when rebilling the net cost to the client
The client reclaims the input VAT directly from HMRC
Input VAT is only reclaimable if the client is also VAT-registered
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume VAT recovery depends on the client's own VAT status — it doesn't. The firm's right to reclaim input VAT depends on the firm being the customer on the supplier's invoice and using the item for its taxable business, not on anything about the client.
testPool.explanation: The firm, as the named customer, reclaims the input VAT it was charged, and separately charges output VAT on the rebilled net amount — the client's own VAT status is irrelevant to either step.

testPool.prompt: A firm arranges for an interpreter to attend a client meeting. The client found and instructed the interpreter directly; the interpreter's invoice for £150 is addressed to the client and states the client's name as the engaging party. The firm pays the £150 from client account as a convenience, then bills the client £150 plus 20% VAT, reasoning that 'the firm handled the payment so VAT applies'. Is this correct?
options: Yes — whenever the firm handles payment, output VAT applies
No — the interpreter's invoice names the client as the engaging party, so this is an agency disbursement and no VAT should be added by the firm
Yes, but only because the amount exceeds £100
No — VAT should have been charged at 5%, not 20%, on a disbursement of this kind
testPool.trapExplanation: The firm's reasoning conflates 'who paid' with 'who contracted'. Handling the payment as a convenience does not change who the supplier's invoice names as customer, which here is the client — so this should have been passed on unchanged with no VAT.
testPool.explanation: Because the interpreter's own invoice identifies the client as the engaging party, this is an agency disbursement regardless of who physically made the payment — the firm's added VAT was wrong.

testPool.prompt: A firm instructs an accident reconstruction expert in its own name for £1,000 plus £200 VAT to support a client's personal injury claim, using the expert's findings directly in preparing the case. What net cost does the disbursement represent to the firm, and what should the firm charge the client?
options: Net cost to firm £1,000 (after reclaiming input VAT); firm rebills £1,000 plus its own £200 output VAT
Net cost to firm £1,200 (no input VAT recovery); firm rebills £1,200 with no further VAT
Net cost to firm £1,000; firm rebills £1,000 with no VAT, since expert fees are VAT-exempt
Net cost to firm £1,200; firm rebills £1,440, adding a further 20% on the gross figure
testPool.explanation: As a principal disbursement, the firm reclaims the £200 input VAT (net cost £1,000) and charges its own £200 output VAT when rebilling — the client is billed £1,200 in total, as part of the firm's own supply, not as a pass-through of the expert's invoice.

testPool.prompt: A supplier's invoice for a disbursement is addressed to the client, and the amount is passed on unchanged with no mark-up — but the firm did use the material for its own advice before passing on the cost. Is HMRC's test satisfied purely by the invoice addressee, ignoring the firm's use of the material?
options: No — the factors are weighed together, and use by the firm for its own purposes counts against treating it as a disbursement even where the invoice names the client
Yes — the invoice addressee alone is always conclusive, regardless of any other factor
No — but only because the amount happened to be passed on unchanged
Yes, provided the firm discloses its use of the material to the client afterwards
testPool.explanation: No single factor is automatically decisive. Use of the item by the firm for its own purposes is one of the indicators HMRC weighs against agency treatment, even where other factors (like the invoice addressee) point the other way — which is exactly why some fact patterns are genuinely borderline.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'the firm paid it' or 'it's on the client's behalf' as the deciding fact. Neither is. The only question that fixes VAT treatment is who the supplier's own invoice names as its customer — check that first, every time.
